Infinite scrolling is a web design technique with both notable benefits and significant drawbacks depending on context, user needs, and implementation. [d1] It can increase user engagement and content discovery, as scrolling has lower interaction cost than clicking, making it well-suited for social media feeds and discovery interfaces. [d3] For eCommerce, it offers fast browsing, works well on mobile and touchscreen devices, and keeps customers engaged longer with continuously displayed products. [d4] However, it works best for easily digestible content and touch-based devices, and can hinder users who are trying to find specific information or who use desktop computers.

On the accessibility front, [d2] infinite scroll is problematic for people with disabilities, including screen reader users who cannot determine if a footer exists and become frustrated by endless content. [d5] Keyboard-only users are also excluded, as they cannot access content inside an infinite scrolling feed even when role=feed is implemented. From a usability perspective, [d6] users find infinite scroll frustrating because it prevents tracking reading progress and resuming from a specific point, unlike pagination. [d7] Etsy's experience showed that infinite scroll removes natural decision points and makes it harder for users to navigate back to remembered items. Finally, [d8] [d9] research and reporting from credible outlets highlight that infinite scroll exploits dopamine reward mechanisms and automaticity, contributing to doom-scrolling, anxiety, information overload, and loss of conscious control—effects that are especially harmful for children, teenagers, and people with mental health conditions.
